## Darboux Criterion for Riemann Integrability

**Setup.** Let $f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be a bounded function. For a partition (division) $P = \{a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n = b\}$ of $[a, b]$, define on each subinterval $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$:

$$m_i = \inf_{x \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]} f(x), \qquad M_i = \sup_{x \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]} f(x).$$

The **lower** and **upper Darboux sums** are

$$L(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i \, \Delta x_i, \qquad U(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} M_i \, \Delta x_i, \qquad \Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}.$$

The **norm** (mesh) of the partition is

$$\|P\| = \max_{1 \le i \le n} \Delta x_i.$$

**Darboux Criterion.** The function $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a, b]$ if and only if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that for every partition $P$ of $[a, b]$ with

$$\|P\| < \delta,$$

the gap between the upper and lower Darboux sums satisfies

$$U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \varepsilon.$$

Equivalently, writing $S(P, f) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(t_i)\,\Delta x_i$ for any choice of sample points $t_i \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]$ (a Riemann sum), the criterion says:

$$\|P\| \to 0 \implies U(P, f) - L(P, f) \to 0,$$

i.e., the upper and lower Darboux sums can be made arbitrarily close to each other by taking the partition fine enough (norm of the division sufficiently small).

**Remark on the quantifier structure.** The criterion is sometimes stated in two equivalent forms:

1. **Norm-controlled form** (stated above): $\forall \varepsilon > 0,\ \exists \delta > 0,\ \forall P$ with $\|P\| < \delta$: $\;U(P,f) - L(P,f) < \varepsilon$.

2. **Partition-existence form**: $\forall \varepsilon > 0,\ \exists P$: $\;U(P, f) - L(P, f) < \varepsilon$.

Both are equivalent for bounded $f$. The norm-controlled form is the one that explicitly involves the norm of the division, as requested in the problem. The equivalence of the two forms relies on the fact that refining a partition can only decrease $U(P, f)$ and increase $L(P, f)$, so that once a single partition makes the gap small, every sufficiently fine refinement (and, by a standard argument, every partition of small enough norm) also makes the gap small.

**Why this characterizes integrability.** The lower and upper Darboux integrals are

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f = \sup_P L(P, f), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f = \inf_P U(P, f).$$

By construction $\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ always. The Darboux criterion asserts exactly that these two coincide, which is the definition of Riemann integrability, with the common value being $\int_a^b f$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
